newsitem.title: UK: Sterling eases against mark, market cautious, thin.
newsitem.headline: Sterling eases against mark, market cautious, thin.

text.p: Sterling drifted downwards against the German mark on Monday after a brief peak following publication of better-than-expected UK public sector debt levels.

Traders said the market was thin and still vulnerable to continuing speculation of a possible German interest rate rise following Tuesday's repo tender or Thursday's meeting of the Bundesbank council, the first since the four-week summer recess.
Cable appeared firmly capped around $1.6140, just below overnight highs and above Friday's late European level of $1.6089/94. It stood at $1.6075/83 at 1005 GMT.
Against the mark it stood at 2.9203/08, one pfennig off session highs of 2.9310.
On the downside, the mark looked to 2.90 where a round number coincides with heavy congestion. On the upside, resistance beckoned at 2.9260 where a downtrend coincides again with heavy congestion.
"These numbers don't hold much fear for us in the present volatile market. We've seen them and been through them all before," Lee Ferridge, currency strategist at Commerzbank, said.
Publication of UK PSBR figures had given sterling a slight fillip after a sluggish start.
The figures showed the government repaid 3.875 billion sterling of public sector debt in July, compared with a level of 1.9 billion pounds generally expected by the market.
Analysts put down the good figures largely to Value Added Tax receipts higher than any previously recorded.
Traders said the market was open to influence from asset market moves after a slide on Wall Street and the London Stock Exchange on Friday.
"Much depends on the Dow. If the Dow opens well, the dollar could move up (against the mark) and pull sterling with it."
The UK FTSE-100 recovered somewhat after the PSBR figures.
The FTSE-100 index made its biggest point loss since 1987 on Friday, wiping out more than two percent of share value.
While the FTSE recouped some of Monday's continued early losses, gilts also firmed, reflecting strength in the U.S. bond market on Friday.

A German government spokesman said on Monday that Chancellor Helmut Kohl remained committed to a punctual launch of the single European currency. On Sunday, Kohl said in a newspaper interview he would not give up his policy of stability "out of enthusiasm for Europe".
